In many cities, libraries are changing their role. In addition to lending books, some now lend useful objects such as tools, cooking equipment, and musical instruments. These places are sometimes called "libraries of things." The idea is simple: people do not need to buy an object if they only use it a few times a year. One such library opened in a small Canadian town. At first, the organizers worried that few residents would use the service. However, within several months, hundreds of people had joined. One popular item was a power drill. Most families need a drill for only a few minutes when fixing furniture or putting up shelves. Instead of buying one, members could borrow it for free. The service has also created unexpected benefits. People often meet neighbors when they pick up or return items. Some members have even started teaching each other how to use tools safely. As a result, the library has become more than a place to borrow things. It has become a place where people share skills and ideas. Of course, there are challenges. Items can break, and staff must check them carefully. The library also needs money to repair or replace damaged equipment. Still, supporters believe the system saves money and reduces waste. If more communities adopt this idea, people may think differently about what they truly need to own.
